summary: Phase 4 of suite deployment mode: myseliasan now forwards live camera video across instances, closing the last documented multi-instance gap. A node opens TWO independent connections to the control plane -- the control channel for commands (made cluster-aware in Phase 2) and a separate media channel carrying camera RTP -- and nothing guarantees they land on the same instance; only the instance holding the media channel could answer a browser's WebRTC offer for that node's cameras, so behind a load balancer a viewer had a 1-in-N chance of landing somewhere that could serve them, and otherwise got "node media channel is not connected" for a camera that was streaming perfectly. The fix forwards the NEGOTIATION, not the media: a browser's SDP offer for a node held elsewhere is passed to the owning instance (new apps/myseliasan/services/media_peer.go: PeerMediaOfferPath, MediaOfferRequest/Reply, PeerClient.ForwardMediaOffer, PeerMediaOfferHandler, reusing the same derived peer token as the command hop), which builds the answer with its own WebRTC engine; the answer carries that instance's own ICE candidates, so the browser then peers with it DIRECTLY and the video never crosses the load balancer or a second instance -- relaying the RTP itself would have doubled bandwidth and added a hop of latency to every frame, to move bytes already designed to go peer-to-peer. apps/myseliasan/services/node_owner.go now builds a second, independently-namespaced ownership registry (NewMediaOwnerRegistry, key prefix mediaowner: vs the control channel's nodeowner:) so a node's media-channel and control-channel claims are tracked and released completely separately -- sharing one namespace would send a camera offer to an instance holding only the command channel, and vice versa, both failing in a way indistinguishable from the node being down. apps/myseliasan/services/media_relay.go gains MediaRelayHub.SetOwnershipHooks, firing the disconnect hook AFTER the connection is torn down so a peer can never observe it as still held here. apps/myseliasan/apis/node_media.go's offer handler now forwards to the owning instance when the node isn't held locally (authorization already happened on the instance the browser reached, before forwarding) and gains AnswerLocalOffer for the receiving side, which deliberately does not re-authorize -- the forwarding instance already resolved the operator's live session and per-node grant, and re-resolving from a role id carried on the wire would be a weaker check. node_peer.go's bearer-token comparison was extracted into a shared constant-time peerTokenMatches so the command hop and the new media hop can never drift into different comparisons. Also included: fleet-rule EDITS now propagate across instances too -- correlator.Save/Delete each call the new announceRulesChanged after their own Reload succeeds, which publishes on node_events.go's new fleet-rules-changed topic (correlator.SetOnRulesChanged, wired end-to-end in app.go); an operator's rule edit or delete now reloads every instance's rule cache, not just the one that served the request. This is unrelated to, and complements, Phase 3's fleet-rule fix (a rule whose CLAUSES span nodes on different instances correctly arms via the existing event bus, about event correlation) -- this one keeps the rule DEFINITION itself in sync after an edit. The call was, briefly during development, wired everywhere (the callback registered, the subscriber listening, the topic defined) except actually invoked from Save/Delete, and because Go does not flag an unused method that state compiled and passed every other test while doing nothing; it is now guarded by a source-level (go/ast) regression test, correlate_announce_test.go, that parses correlate_crud.go and fails if either call site is ever removed -- a feature whose failure mode is silence needs a test that checks the call was made, not one that infers it from a downstream effect. The setup wizard's deployment caveat list is now down to one item: the three now-closed caveats (node liveness/screens, live notification bell/cross-instance rules, live camera video) were removed from all four locales, and the shared deploy.caveatsTitle/caveatsBody copy was reworded in all four languages from 'Not ready for multiple instances yet' to 'One thing to know first' / a single-remaining-point framing, since an overstated warning is one operators learn to discount.
compatibility: With cluster.advertiseUrl empty (the default, and the value in every existing config.json) nothing changes for a single instance: the media-owner registry degenerates to a local-only map, mediaForward is never built (nil), the peer media-offer endpoint is never mounted, and every camera negotiates exactly as it always has; PublishRulesChanged/SubscribeRulesChanged are likewise no-ops against the default in-process event bus, so an unclustered install's rule Save/Delete behaves exactly as before (Reload only). Enabling this requires nothing beyond what Phase 2 clustering already needs (cluster.advertiseUrl set per instance, shared jwt.secret) -- no new config field was added. Only the WebRTC negotiation is forwarded between instances; the media itself always flows directly from the browser to the instance actually holding the node's media channel, so each instance still needs its own reachable address and UDP port for live video, exactly as the operator checklist has required since deployment mode was introduced -- this change is what makes that requirement load-bearing rather than aspirational. Verification status: the media-forwarding hop is unit-tested at its own seam (8 cases covering the round-trip, auth, not-connected propagation, payload validation, an unreachable owner, and independent tracking/release of control-channel vs media-channel ownership), but it was NOT exercised end-to-end with real cameras -- the live two-instance bench used a mypintusan door controller, which has no cameras, so cross-instance video has not actually been watched in a browser. The fleet-rule-reload-propagation fix is source-level regression-tested (correlate_announce_test.go) and the full suite is green; it was not separately exercised on the two-instance live bench either, but is a straightforward extension of the already-live-verified Phase 3 event bus.
